2: Analysis and design of synchronous sequential circuits

questions.q: Simplify F(A, B, C, D) = sum of minterms (0, 1, 2, 5, 8, 9, 10) using a Karnaugh map. Show the groups you form.
Why is the Quine-McCluskey method preferred over the K-map for functions of six or more variables?
questions.model: K-maps become hard to draw and read beyond 4-5 variables and depend on visual grouping; Quine-McCluskey is a tabular, systematic procedure (prime implicants, then a prime implicant chart) that can be programmed.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of 2-input NAND gates needed to implement a 2-input XOR gate?
questions.model: Four NAND gates: N1 = (AB)', then A XOR B = ((A N1)' (B N1)')'.

questions.q: Implement F(A, B, C) = sum of minterms (1, 2, 6, 7) with a 4:1 multiplexer using A and B as select lines. Give the four data inputs.
questions.model: AB = 00: minterms 0, 1 -> I0 = C. AB = 01: minterms 2, 3 -> I1 = C'. AB = 10: minterms 4, 5 -> I2 = 0. AB = 11: minterms 6, 7 -> I3 = 1.

questions.q: True or False: In an SR latch built from NOR gates, the input combination S = 1, R = 1 is not allowed.
questions.model: True: both outputs are forced to 0 and the next state is unpredictable when the inputs return to 0.

questions.q: The characteristic equation of the JK flip-flop is Q(next) = ___, and that of the T flip-flop is Q(next) = ___.
questions.model: JK: Q+ = JQ' + K'Q; T: Q+ = T XOR Q.

questions.q: Convert a JK flip-flop into a T flip-flop. Show the excitation table you use and the resulting connections.
questions.model: T = 0 keeps Q (J = K = 0), T = 1 toggles (J = K = 1). From the excitation tables, J = T and K = T: connect both J and K to T.

questions.t: Analysis and design of synchronous sequential circuits
questions.q: Design a Mealy sequence detector that outputs 1 when the overlapping sequence 101 is detected on a serial input, using D flip-flops. Give the state diagram, state table and flip-flop input equations.
How many flip-flops are needed to build a mod-12 counter?

A design needs serial-to-parallel conversion, parallel loading and shifting in both directions in one component. Evaluate whether a universal shift register meets this need and describe how its mode-select inputs are used.
questions.model: Yes: a universal shift register supports hold, shift left, shift right and parallel load, chosen by two mode-select lines (00 hold, 01 right, 10 left, 11 load) through a 4:1 mux in front of each flip-flop; parallel outputs give serial-to-parallel conversion.

questions.q: Read the assertion and reason about RISC and CISC machines and choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: RISC processors use fixed-length instructions to simplify decoding and pipelining.
questions.reason: RISC processors follow a load/store architecture in which only load and store instructions access memory.
questions.model: Both are true, but load/store access does not explain the use of fixed-length instruction encoding.

questions.q: 40% of a program's execution time can be parallelised perfectly. Using Amdahl's law, what is the overall speed-up on 4 processors? (Give two decimal places.)
When 12.375 is stored in IEEE 754 single precision, what is the decimal value of its 8-bit biased exponent field?
In which addressing mode does the instruction name a register that holds the memory address of the operand?
questions.model: Register indirect: the register contains the effective address.

questions.q: A 5-stage instruction pipeline executes 100 instructions with no stalls. How many clock cycles are needed?
For ADD R1, R2, R3 followed by SUB R4, R1, R5 in a 5-stage pipeline, identify the hazard, explain why it occurs, and show how forwarding removes or reduces the stall.
questions.model: A RAW data hazard: SUB reads R1 before ADD writes it back. Forwarding passes ADD's ALU result from the EX/MEM latch directly to SUB's ALU input, removing the stall.

questions.q: Explain temporal and spatial locality with one programming example of each, and state why locality makes caches effective.
questions.model: Temporal: recently used items are used again (a loop counter). Spatial: nearby addresses are used soon (sequential array access). Caches keep recent data and whole blocks, so most accesses hit.

questions.q: A direct-mapped cache of 64 KB has 16-byte blocks and the processor uses 32-bit byte addresses. How many bits are in the tag field?
questions.model: Offset 4 bits; 64 KB / 16 B = 4096 lines, index 12 bits; tag = 32 - 12 - 4 = 16 bits.

questions.q: A cache has a hit ratio of 0.9 and an access time of 10 ns; a miss costs the 10 ns cache look-up plus 100 ns to main memory. What is the average memory access time in ns?
For each device in the case, choose programmed I/O, interrupt-driven I/O or DMA and justify your choice in terms of CPU utilisation and data rate.
questions.case: An embedded controller must handle (1) a keyboard producing a few characters per second, (2) a disk transferring 4 KB blocks at high speed, and (3) a temperature sensor read once at start-up during system self-test.
questions.model: Keyboard: interrupt-driven, as events are rare and polling would waste CPU time. Disk: DMA, so whole blocks move to memory without the CPU handling each word; one interrupt at the end. Sensor at start-up: programmed I/O is simplest, the CPU has nothing else to do and it happens once.
